title: Anendesak / Eaton's Neck
summary: A Huntington-area tract name tied to Eaton's Neck, Eader Necks Beach, and the Assawanama/Fresh Pond boundary landscape.
why_this_matters: Anendesak matters even though its exact meaning has not been identified, because the recorded name preserves a Native layer of Huntington-area geography beneath the later English name Eaton's Neck. Its survival in written records shows how Indigenous place knowledge can remain visible even when translation is uncertain. The name keeps attention on a North Shore neck of land that carried Native meaning before later colonial ownership names took over.
introduction_content: Anendesak is recorded as a name for a tract near Huntington, described in English as Eader Necks Beach and associated with Eaton's Neck. The form is treated cautiously because the meaning is uncertain and the recorded word may be corrupted.
history_content: Anendesak with the Eaton's Neck and Fresh Pond landscape remain connected here, with detailed dated claims in the Historic Timeline.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Anendesak and Anendesack. William Wallace Tooker did not identify a meaning and cautioned that the form was probably badly corrupted.

Why Place Names Matter

“All the geographical names of the Earth put together represent an immeasurable body of human experience and insight.”

— United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names, Manual for the National Standardization of Geographical Names (2006), PDF page 132
